lesson.title: Which graph?
lesson.body: A bar graph compares amounts in categories. A line graph shows how an amount changes over time. A pie graph shows how one whole is split into parts. A double bar or double line graph shows two sets at once, with a key to tell them apart.

lesson.title: Reading a value
lesson.body: Find the category along the bottom. Then follow the top of the bar, or the point on the line, across to the numbers on the side. Every bar and point here sits on a gridline, so you can read it exactly.

lesson.title: How many more?
lesson.body: To compare two bars, take the shorter from the taller. How many more is a difference, never a sum.

lesson.title: Change on a line
lesson.body: When a line goes up from one point to the next, the amount increased; when it goes down, it decreased. The size of the change is the difference between the two points.

lesson.title: Look at the whole graph
lesson.body: A conclusion comes from the whole graph, not one bar. Where is the gap between the two sets biggest? Does the line rise all the way, or turn?

lesson.title: The average
lesson.body: The average is the total shared equally: add all the values, then divide by how many there are. Five days with a total of 150 is 150 ÷ 5 = 30 a day.

lesson.title: One whole
lesson.body: A pie graph is one whole. Its percents add up to 100%, and the angles at its centre add up to 360°.

lesson.title: Percent and angle
lesson.body: 1% of the circle is 360° ÷ 100 = 3.6°. So 25% is 25 × 3.6 = 90°, and an angle of 72° is 72 ÷ 3.6 = 20%.

lesson.title: What a slice stands for
lesson.body: A slice stands for its part of the whole amount. A 30% slice of ₱500 is 30 × ₱5 = ₱150; a 90° slice of 40 pupils is 90/360 = 1/4 of them, 10 pupils.

lesson.title: Tables
lesson.body: A table gives exact values in rows and columns, as many websites and news reports do. Find the row, then the column, and the value is where they meet.
